situation:
You are the human resources manager at STONEHILL CONSTRUCTION, a residential and light commercial building contractor. The company president (judge), the third generation of the founding family to run the business, has asked you to recommend how STONEHILL should staff the coming building season and which work it should take on.

STONEHILL builds from March through November and releases most field crews for the winter. Tradespeople come back each spring because the company calls the same crews first, and that callback record is the reason experienced framers stay with a seasonal employer at all. Six framing crews is the most the company's current supervisors and equipment can keep working at one time.

This spring the book of work runs past that limit. Two long-standing residential builders hold spring schedules STONEHILL has already committed to. Two new commercial customers, larger than anything the company has built before, are waiting on an answer. Taking all four means hiring and training two more crews through COASTAL TRADES STAFFING and releasing them in November with the rest.

Hiring the two additional crews carries training and wage costs the company pays out and then releases in November, and a fall layoff of crews hired months earlier is what damages the callback record the returning tradespeople count on. Declining the two new commercial customers holds the season steady and hands that work to a competitor, and those customers may not ask again.

The company president (judge) wants your recommendation on how many crews to bring on, which customers to serve, and how the company should answer the customers who are still waiting. The company president (judge) will greet you, hear your ideas and ask questions. When you have finished answering, the company president (judge) will thank you for your work.
